tagline: Neither vampire nor squid, but a gentle snow-eater
summary: Despite its name, the vampire squid is neither a vampire nor a squid but the last surviving member of an ancient cephalopod group. It drifts through the low-oxygen twilight zone, gathering 'marine snow', the sinking debris of the waters above, with two long sticky filaments.

stats.size: Up to about 30 cm total length
stats.range: Worldwide in tropical and temperate seas
stats.diet: Marine snow (sinking organic debris); also small zooplankton
stats.conservation: No IUCN assessment found in sources checked

facts.title: A living fossil
facts.text: Its scientific name means 'vampire squid from hell', yet it is the only living member of its family and the last survivor of an ancient lineage, distinct from both squids and octopuses.

facts.title: Mucus dumplings
facts.text: It traps falling marine snow on two sticky filaments, pulls them through its arms, and wraps the particles in mucus before passing the 'dumpling' to its mouth. It is the only cephalopod known to feed mainly as a scavenger.

facts.title: The pineapple pose
facts.text: When threatened it flips its webbed arms up over its body like a cloak, showing spiky-looking fleshy cirri. If danger persists, its arm tips glow blue, and it can release a glowing cloud instead of ink.

facts.title: Built for low oxygen
facts.text: It thrives in the oxygen minimum zone, where few predators can follow. A very slow metabolism and blood with an unusually high affinity for oxygen help it get by.

facts.title: Many spawnings
facts.text: Unlike most cephalopods, which breed once and die, female vampire squid appear to spawn repeatedly, releasing a few eggs at a time.

references.title: Vampire squid — Animals of the Deep
